newsitem.title: USA: CBO seen forecasting stable U.S. growth.
newsitem.headline: CBO seen forecasting stable U.S. growth.

text.p: The Congressional Budget Office is expected to forecast that the U.S. economy will stay on its current course with a 2.1-2.2 percent growth rate for the coming year, congressional sources said Tuesday.
With the economy generally at what economists consider full employment and no immediate threat of a recession, CBO expects the economy to continue on its current path, the sources said.

Last month the Commerce Department reported third quarter 1996 gross domestic product grew at a 2.0 percent annual rate, down from 4.7 percent in the second quarter. In May CBO forecast GDP at 2.0 percent for calendar 1996 and 1.9 percent for 1997.
CBO is expected to forecast an unemployment rate close to the 5.8 percent rate for 1996 that it saw in its May report.
For November, the Labor Department reported unemployment at 5.4 percent, up from 5.2 percent the previous month.
CBO, a non-partisan economic and budget analysis agency, is to finish work this week on new forecasts of economic growth, unemployment, interest rates and inflation.
The CBO's economic assumptions are the foundation for the agency's estimates of individual and corporate income, federal spending, tax revenues and the government's budget deficit.

These estimates will be used by Congress and the White House in negotiating the budget for the coming 1998 fiscal year. Known as "technical assumptions", the estimates are expected to be given to the White House this month.

A forecast of a stable economic picture would be in line with the Federal Reserve's latest Beige Book summary of national economic activity which suggested a slow but steady expansion, rather than an acceleration, lay ahead.

"Moderate economic growth continues to be reported in nearly all Federal Reserve districts," said the summary prepared by the Philadelphia Fed for the Dec. 17 meeting of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, which will plot interest-rate strategy.

While CBO's forecasts have generally been more conservative than those produced by the White House's Office of Management and Budget (OMB), this year the economy performed closer to White House forecasts.

Chiefly due to lower health care costs and unexpectedly high tax revenues, the budget deficit for fiscal 1996, which ended September 30, fell to $107 million, $37 billion below the CBO's May forecast.

However, the CBO is still expected to foresee the deficit rising in the current 1997 fiscal year, absent a balanced budget agreement between the White House and Congress which cuts spending or brings in more taxes. CBO's August report forecast the 1997 deficit rising to $155 billion. CBO did not revise its economic forecasts in August.

While 1997 will still see some added benefit from lower health care expenses for Medicare and Medicaid for the elderly and poor, this is expected to level off and, in later years the rising elderly population will require higher spending.
In addition, last year's rise in revenues, still the subject of speculation, may not fully carry over into 1997.
